title: Numerical differentiation and integration
subtitle: Slopes from differences, areas from slices, and how error shrinks as the slices get thinner.

sections.title: Numerical differentiation
sections.body:
How do you find a slope when all you have is a table of numbers? You take a tiny step and divide. From the definition f′(x) ≈ [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h (the forward difference, error O(h)); the central difference [f(x + h) − f(x − h)]/(2h) has error O(h²), which is much better.

Beware the trap of making h too small. Shrinking h reduces truncation error but amplifies round-off error, so there is an optimal h (around 10⁻⁵ for double precision central differences). Try the derivative of sin x at x = 0 with h = 0.1. Central: [sin 0.1 − sin(−0.1)]/0.2 = 0.19967/0.2 = 0.99833 (true 1). The forward difference gives sin 0.1 / 0.1 = 0.99833 too at this point (symmetry); at other x the central is much better. The central difference is the more accurate formula for the same h.

worked.why: Estimate the derivative of sin x at x = 0 with h = 0.1.
Forward: sin 0.1 / 0.1 = 0.99833 too at this point (symmetry); at other x the central is much better.

questions.prompt: Which difference formula is more accurate for the same h?

keynotes: The forward difference [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h has error O(h); the central difference [f(x + h) − f(x − h)]/(2h) has error O(h²).
Shrinking h reduces truncation error but amplifies round-off error, so there is an optimal h, around 10⁻⁵ for double precision central differences.
For sin x at x = 0 with h = 0.1 the central difference gives 0.99833 against the true 1.

sections.title: The trapezoidal rule
sections.body:
To find an area under a curve, slice it into strips and add them up. The trapezoidal rule replaces the curve over each subinterval by a straight line: ∫f ≈ h[½f₀ + f₁ + … + fn−1 + ½fₙ]. The error is O(h²): halve h, quarter the error.

Test it on ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2. With n = 4 strips, h = π/4 and the function values at 0, π/4, π/2, 3π/4, π are 0, .7071, 1, .7071, 0. The trapezoid sum is h[½(0)+.7071+1+.7071+½(0)] = (π/4)(2.4142) = 1.896119 (error 1.04e-1). With 32 intervals you get 1.998393. Each frame of the figure doubles the strips and the error drops. Halving the step size reduces the error by about a factor of four.

worked.why: n = 4 strips on [0, π]: h = π/4 and the function values at 0, π/4, π/2, 3π/4, π.

questions.prompt: Halving the step size of the trapezoidal rule reduces the error by about…

figures.note: Each frame doubles the number of strips; the error drops.

keynotes: The trapezoidal rule is ∫f ≈ h[½f₀ + f₁ + … + f(n−1) + ½fₙ] with error O(h²): halve h, quarter the error.
For ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2, four intervals give 1.896119 (error 1.04e-1) and 32 intervals give 1.998393.
With n = 4, h = π/4 and the sum is (π/4)(2.4142), which gives 1.896119.

sections.title: Simpson’s rule
sections.body:
Why use straight lines when you can use curves? Simpson’s rule fits a parabola through each pair of strips: ∫f ≈ (h/3)[f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + 4f₃ + … + fₙ], with n even. The error is O(h⁴) and the rule is exact for cubics.

Same four intervals, same function: with h = π/4 the coefficients 1, 4, 2, 4, 1 on the values 0, .7071, 1, .7071, 0 give (h/3)(0+4(.7071)+2(1)+4(.7071)+0) = 2.0046. Simpson gives 2.00456 (error 4.56e-3), much better than the trapezoid’s 1.04e-1. The parabolic arcs follow the curve closely in the figure. Simpson’s 1/3 rule requires an even number of intervals.

worked.why: n = 4, h = π/4; coefficients 1, 4, 2, 4, 1 on the values 0, .7071, 1, .7071, 0.

figures.caption: Figure 4.3.1 — Simpson’s 1/3 rule
figures.note: Parabolic arcs follow the curve closely.

problems.prompt: Approximate ∫₀^π sin x dx with n = 4 using the trapezoid and Simpson rules. Compare with 2.

keynotes: Simpson’s rule fits a parabola through each pair of strips: ∫f ≈ (h/3)[f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + 4f₃ + … + fₙ], with n even.
Its error is O(h⁴) and the rule is exact for cubics.
Four intervals give 2.00456 (error 4.56e-3), much better than the trapezoid’s 1.04e-1.

sections.title: Richardson extrapolation and Romberg
sections.body:
Here is a trick for the lazy and clever. If you have two trapezoid estimates, with steps h and h/2, you can combine them to cancel the biggest error term. If the trapezoid error is C·h², then better = [4T(h/2) − T(h)]/3 cancels the h² term. Repeating gives Romberg integration, a triangle of ever better values.

Try it: T(π/2) = 1.5708 (n = 2) and T(π/4) = 1.8961 (n = 4). Extrapolate: (4(1.8961) − 1.5708)/3 = 2.0046. Hold on, that is exactly Simpson’s answer. Indeed, one extrapolation of the trapezoid rule equals Simpson’s rule.

questions.prompt: Richardson extrapolation of two trapezoid estimates gives…

keynotes: If the trapezoid error is C·h², then [4T(h/2) − T(h)]/3 cancels the h² term; repeating gives Romberg integration.
One extrapolation of the trapezoid rule equals Simpson’s rule.

sections.title: Gauss quadrature (idea)
sections.body:
Newton–Cotes rules fix equally spaced nodes, but what if you could choose the points too? Gaussian quadrature chooses both nodes and weights: an n-point rule is exact for polynomials up to degree 2n − 1. The two-point rule on [−1, 1] uses nodes ±1/√3 with weights 1 and 1.

Test it by integrating x² on [−1, 1] with the 2-point Gauss rule: 1·⅓ + 1·⅓ = 2/3, the exact value. Two points, and a degree-3 polynomial is integrated perfectly. You can see why choosing the nodes is so powerful.

worked.why: Integrate x² on [−1, 1] by the 2-point Gauss rule.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Two lines to keep.

  • Central difference O(h²); trapezoid O(h²); Simpson O(h⁴), n even.
  • Extrapolate to cancel leading error terms.
keynotes: Central difference and trapezoid are O(h²); Simpson is O(h⁴) with n even.
Extrapolate to cancel leading error terms.
